topic: Tennis elbow: grip, load and patience

slides.headline: Tennis elbow? You don't need to play
slides.sub: Grip, load and patience: how outer elbow pain usually settles.

slides.title: What it usually is
slides.body: Lateral elbow pain comes from the tendons that attach on the outside of the elbow. It's common in people who grip a lot: mouse users, tradies, gym-goers and, yes, tennis players.

slides.title: Grip is the giveaway
slides.body: Pain gripping a kettle, opening jars or shaking hands is typical. Use a lighter grip where you can, lift with your palm facing up, and take regular micro-breaks from the mouse.

slides.title: Load it, don't baby it
slides.body: Tendons respond to gradual loading. Slow wrist exercises with a light dumbbell or band are a common starting point. Mild discomfort that settles by the next day is usually okay.

slides.title: Patience is part of the plan
slides.body: Tennis elbow is often slow to settle and can take months. Research suggests steady, progressive exercise helps most people improve over time, so stick with it even when progress feels slow.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall or a big lift, swelling or a clunk in the joint, numbness or tingling into the hand, or weakness when gripping. These are worth a proper assessment.

caption:
You don't have to play tennis to get tennis elbow. A mouse, a tool or the gym is a far more common trigger.

Outer elbow pain comes from the tendons on the outside of the elbow, and gripping is usually what sets it off. Small changes help: a lighter grip, lifting with your palm up and micro-breaks at the desk.

Tendons respond to gradual loading, so slow wrist exercises are a common starting point. It can take months to settle, and steady, progressive work usually wins out.

Numbness into the hand or pain after a fall is worth checking.
